content: The cost-effectiveness of implementing HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) testing varies significantly across lowand middle-income countries due to differences in drug costs and thresholds for cost-effectiveness. A survey revealed that 57% of healthcare workers reported no access to routine HIVDR testing in their clinics, and only 14% of respondents from these countries conducted HIVDR testing before initiating treatment. The primary challenges to introducing pretreatment HIVDR testing included difficulties in interpreting results, delays in receiving results, and challenges in retaining patients in care during the waiting period. Program managers highlighted additional barriers, such as the high cost of testing, insufficient laboratory capacity, and a lack of trained personnel. When presented with options to address pretreatment HIVDR, respondents equally preferred introducing an alternative first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen or implementing HIVDR testing for all treatment initiators to guide regimen selection. Although explicit questions about acceptability, values, and preferences regarding pretreatment HIVDR testing were not asked of people living with HIV, civil society representatives emphasized the importance of equitable care standards to minimize disparities across geographic settings. Pretreatment HIVDR testing is not widely available in lowand middle-income countries. A 2017 WHO-led survey found that only 31% of program managers in ten such countries considered pretreatment HIVDR testing feasible or somewhat feasible. Key challenges included cost, result interpretation, delays in receiving results, ensuring patient retention during the waiting period, and maintaining a consistent supply of alternative first-line ART regimens. Countries with a pretreatment HIVDR prevalence of 10% or higher among individuals initiating first-line ART are strongly advised to consider alternative first-line regimens that do not include non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). If a non-NNRTI regimen cannot be implemented at the population level, pretreatment HIVDR testing can guide regimen selection. The threshold of 10% for triggering a public health response was established based on evidence showing the negative impact of pretreatment HIVDR on treatment outcomes when NNRTI-based regimens are used. Modeling data also demonstrated the increasing benefits of transitioning to dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens as pretreatment HIVDR prevalence rises. Delaying action at or above the 10% threshold was deemed unjustifiable due to the predicted benefits of transitioning to DTG, including reduced costs and improved treatment outcomes. To assess national pretreatment HIVDR prevalence, WHO recommends conducting surveys using standardized methods. These surveys, which cost approximately $240,000 for a sample size of 460 specimens, provide nationally representative data and are considered a high-priority activity for countries scaling up ART programs. The surveys should be repeated every three years to monitor trends and inform programmatic decisions. The implementation of pretreatment HIVDR testing requires robust laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, and logistical support. Strengthening treatment literacy, adherence support, and retention in care is critical to minimizing HIVDR emergence. Research gaps remain in understanding the long-term efficacy and safety of DTG, the impact of pretreatment HIVDR on DTG-based regimens, and the clinical implications of specific drug resistance mutations. Studies are also needed to optimize the introduction of DTG in lowand middle-income countries and to develop innovative strategies for preventing HIVDR.
